questions.explanation: The 10-year yield is the main reference for many consumer and corporate loan rates, and it rose 6 basis points to 4.96%. The tempting last option is wrong because yields feed through to household borrowing costs.
options: It determines company profits directly through sales tax
It sets the price of oil, so fuel costs rise for consumers
It is the benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt, so borrowing stays expensive
It only affects bond traders and has little effect on consumers
questions.prompt: The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.96%. Why does that matter well beyond the government's own borrowing?

questions.explanation: Iran says it will ease Hormuz energy shipping and return to formal talks only after the US lifts its blockade. Oil stays above $100 because no deal exists yet and the strait remains restricted.
options: The US must lift its economic blockade
OPEC+ must raise production targets
Brent must fall below $100 a barrel
Israel must sign a trade deal
questions.prompt: Brent fell more than 7% on Monday on reports Iran cleared the way for talks, yet it still settled near $103.60 on Tuesday. What does Iran say must happen before it eases shipping through Hormuz?

questions.explanation: $8.5B divided by $13.4B is about 63%, up from a smaller share as data center sales grew 97%. That makes AMD's results depend more on AI infrastructure spending than on PCs.
options: About 25%
About 45%
About 63%
About 85%
questions.prompt: AMD's data center revenue was $8.5B out of $13.4B in total. Roughly what share of AMD's revenue does the data center segment now represent?

questions.explanation: LNG plants cost $10B or more, so lenders want committed offtake before they lend. The contracts secure revenue but do not stop spot prices moving or remove construction risk.
options: They remove all construction and cost risk from the project
They guarantee that the spot price of LNG will never fall
They let the developer avoid building any shipping or terminals
Lenders will finance a multi-billion-dollar plant only against years of committed buyers
questions.prompt: QatarEnergy signed a 20-year deal to buy up to 3 Mtpa of LNG from Woodside's Louisiana project. Why do such long-term contracts matter to a developer?

questions.explanation: A goodwill impairment lowers the book value of past acquisitions without spending cash. Adjusted EPS was $1.75, savings targets doubled to $1B and a $500M buyback was planned, which outweighed the accounting loss.
options: Goodwill write-downs always signal that a company's earnings are about to rise
The write-down does not change cash flow, and investors focused on the $1B savings target and buyback restart
Investors ignored the results because the company missed its revenue forecast
The write-down raised Fiserv's merchant operating margin
questions.prompt: Fiserv booked a $6.45B non-cash goodwill impairment, producing a GAAP loss of $11.17 a share, yet its shares rose about 12%. What best explains the reaction?

questions.explanation: Ferrari earns more by increasing what each customer pays than by selling more cars. Shipments fell because of weaker sales to the Americas and China, but its order book now extends into 2028.
options: Large government subsidies for sports cars
A large increase in the number of cars it sells to China
A sharp cut in the prices of its entry models
Higher revenue per car from personalization and special models, with an order book into 2028
questions.prompt: Ferrari delivered 318 fewer cars over nine months, yet raised its 2026 guidance for a second straight quarter. What best explains this?

questions.explanation: An integrated company earns in several places, so refining and LNG can carry the result when crude prices dip. Weather was a drag: refinery utilisation fell to 96% from 102% partly because of low Rhine water levels.
options: Lower tax payments
Higher refining margins and higher realised LNG prices
Selling its upstream assets
Smaller share buybacks
questions.prompt: Shell's adjusted earnings rose to $10.8B from $5.4B a year earlier even though realised liquids prices fell from the prior quarter. What offset the weaker upstream prices?

questions.explanation: Starbucks deconsolidated China after the joint venture deal, where it keeps a 40% stake and now books equity income rather than store sales. Transactions rose 1.8% and average ticket 5.2%, and only about 250 North American stores closed.
options: It closed most of its US stores
Customers bought fewer drinks but paid far more
A sales-tax change reduced reported revenue
It moved China retail into a licensed joint venture, so those sales left its revenue
questions.prompt: Starbucks' revenue fell 4% to $9.1B even though global same-store sales rose 7.2%. What explains the gap?

questions.explanation: Eliquis grew 25% and revenue guidance rose, so demand was not the problem. The EPS cut came mainly from acquired research and licensing charges, about $0.60 per share, which is a cost of building the pipeline.
options: A fall in Eliquis sales
Weaker US demand for its medicines
Charges for acquired research and licensing deals
A higher corporate tax rate
questions.prompt: Bristol Myers raised its 2026 revenue outlook to about $49.75-50.25B but cut EPS guidance to $6.35-6.55. What mainly explains the lower earnings outlook?

questions.explanation: Plants, engineering and tooling cost roughly the same whatever the volume, so extra sales add profit while lost sales cut deeply. That is why mass-market EBIT margins are only about 5% to 10%.
options: High fixed costs for plants, engineering and tooling that stay the same when sales fall
Raw materials that are free when demand is low
Dealers that pay automakers in advance for all vehicles
Labor costs that vanish when production slows
questions.prompt: Mass-market automakers earn thin average margins and their profits swing sharply with sales volume. What feature of their cost structure explains this?

extra.explanation: With no agreement and Iran tying Hormuz shipping to the US lifting its blockade, prices move several dollars on talk headlines. A real reopening would shift profits quickly between producers and fuel buyers.
options: Oil prices follow US interest rates closely
Prices carry a war premium and swing on headlines about talks and the Strait of Hormuz
Supply has returned to normal after the blockade
Demand has collapsed in all regions
extra.prompt: Brent settled at $103.60 on Tuesday and traded near $97 on Thursday, with no peace deal reached. What does the price movement show?

extra.explanation: AppLovin's software matches advertisers with mobile apps and games and it keeps a cut of the spending it directs, so revenue grows with ad performance.
options: Monthly subscriptions from app users
A share of advertiser spending its software directs to apps and games
Selling smartphones
Charging apps for cloud storage
extra.prompt: AppLovin's revenue rose 55% to about $2.185 billion, above its own $2.055 to $2.085 billion guide. What does AppLovin mainly earn money from?

extra.explanation: Climate change, water scarcity and disease make harvests and prices volatile. Combining production and the brand gives the owners more control over supply and shelf price.
options: Supply swings with weather, disease and water, so prices and margins swing too
Olive oil demand is fixed by law
Prices never change
Bottling is the only profitable step
extra.prompt: Dcoop and Acesur, two Spanish olive oil producers, will each own 50% of Deoleo. Which feature of olive oil markets makes owning both growing and bottling attractive?

extra.explanation: Brokers are asset-light: they arrange moves on other firms' vehicles and keep the difference between the shipper's rate and the carrier's rate. That spread widens when capacity is tight.
options: It earns the spread between what shippers pay and what carriers charge
It owns a large fleet of trucks
It charges ports a fee for each ship
It sells diesel fuel
extra.prompt: Which best describes how a freight broker makes money?

extra.explanation: Tariffs raise input costs for importers, so rolling them back helps them, while protected domestic producers lose some price support. Changes are unlikely before January and the president keeps wide trade powers.
options: Protected domestic producers that compete with imports
Companies that import heavily, such as retailers and manufacturers
Chinese tech firms only
Rare earth miners
extra.prompt: A Democratic Congress takes office in January, and removing tariffs is high on its agenda. Which companies would gain most if tariffs were rolled back?

questions.explanation: Hyperscalers can wait out stricter rules or buy capacity from weaker operators, while a debt-funded provider faces wider spreads: CoreWeave's credit default swap spread passed 1,100 basis points. The projects are not all exempt, since only those already under construction reportedly are.
options: Microsoft and Amazon build fewer data centers than CoreWeave
Large cloud providers have diversified revenue and internal cash flow, while CoreWeave relies on borrowing that gets costlier
CoreWeave's projects are all exempt from the proposed rules
Investors expect permitting rules to apply only to Microsoft and Amazon
questions.prompt: After the midterms, Microsoft and Amazon rose over 6% while CoreWeave fell about 10% as data center permitting risk rose. What best explains the split?

questions.explanation: CVS says independence gives each business a focused agenda and its own capital structure. Insurance and benefit management earn premiums and fees, while stores depend on traffic and thin dispensing margins. The split is meant to be tax-free and does not by itself change revenue.
options: Pharmacies and insurers are required by law to have the same owner
Insurance and pharmacy stores must merge to cut taxes
The split will lift the company's revenue above $420 billion
The two halves have different economics and regulation, so each can pursue its own strategy and capital structure
questions.prompt: CVS plans to separate Aetna and Caremark from its roughly 9,000 pharmacies. What is the main business logic?

questions.explanation: The expansion adds about 225 million pounds a year, lifting output above 400 million pounds. The 400 million figure is the new total, not the addition. The budget is about 30% above a 2023 estimate of $3.5 billion.
options: About 225 million pounds
About 50 million pounds
About 1 billion pounds
About 400 million pounds
questions.prompt: Freeport-McMoRan approved a $4.5 billion expansion of its Bagdad mine. About how much copper per year will it add?

questions.explanation: The companies see an opening to sell a unified design package to the large majority of projects that now use only one of their products. They guide to more than $100 million in annual synergies. The deal is all-stock, and Shoals holders will own about 65%, not 35%.
options: Shoals holders will own only about 35% of the company
Only about 20% of projects used both companies' products, so there is room to cross-sell
Both companies already sell their products as a bundle on most projects
The deal was financed with cash instead of stock
questions.prompt: Array Technologies (solar trackers) is merging with Shoals (electrical connection systems). Which fact best explains the revenue opportunity?

questions.explanation: Profit rising faster than bookings is operating leverage: a large part of the cost base is fixed, so growth drops through to profit. Non-GAAP operating income reached 3.9% of gross bookings, or $2.3 billion.
options: Uber raised the share of bookings paid out to drivers
Costs grew more slowly than bookings, so each extra dollar of activity added more profit
Uber's bookings were mostly recorded in the previous year
Fuel prices fell sharply in the quarter
questions.prompt: Uber's non-GAAP operating income grew 38% while gross bookings grew 20%. What does this gap show?

questions.explanation: Datadog bills mostly according to how much customers use its tools, so reduced use lowers revenue with no cancellation. That makes it more sensitive to a few large customers than a fixed-fee subscription would be.
options: The customer has cancelled its contract and must pay a penalty
Datadog's costs rise automatically when a customer leaves
Its guidance excluded that customer
Revenue is billed mostly on usage, so one big customer using less cuts revenue directly
questions.prompt: Datadog's revenue grew 35% to about $1.2 billion, yet its filing warns that growth may slow. Why does lower usage by its largest customer matter so much?

questions.explanation: An integrated company owns both production and refining. Upstream earned $7.1B, down on lower prices, while refining margins and strong diesel yields lifted Energy Products. A pure producer would not have that offset.
options: Refining and fuel margins can widen when crude prices ease, offsetting weaker production profits
Lower crude prices raise its output automatically
Governments pay refiners subsidies whenever crude falls
Its chemicals prices are fixed by ten-year contracts
questions.prompt: ExxonMobil's upstream earnings fell in Q3 2026 while Energy Products (refining) rose to $7.2B, lifting adjusted earnings to $17.5B. Why can an integrated oil company's profit hold up when crude eases?

questions.explanation: When spending outgrows income, the gap comes from savings, and the saving rate dropped from 4.0% to 3.8%. Strong growth with inflation at 3.6% also keeps the Fed leaning toward holding or raising rates.
options: Households are building a larger cushion
Consumers are cutting back sharply
Spending growth is partly funded by drawing down savings, which cannot continue indefinitely
Income is growing faster than spending
questions.prompt: Third-quarter GDP grew 3.4%, but income rose 0.2% while spending rose 0.5% and the saving rate fell to 3.8%. What does this imply?

questions.explanation: Once a network is built, each added user and gigabyte brings revenue with little extra cost, so profit grows faster than sales. Jio added 9.1 million subscribers and data traffic rose 22%.
options: Jio cut the number of subscribers
Government subsidies replaced customer fees
Jio sold its network to a tower company
Network costs are mostly fixed, so extra subscribers and data use add profit at low cost
questions.prompt: Jio's revenue rose 11% but EBITDA rose 17%, lifting the margin to 54.1%. What explains this?

questions.explanation: In a commodity business producers cannot set price, so profit is price minus cost. Low-cost producers stay profitable when prices drop while high-cost rivals lose money and eventually cut output.
options: They receive higher prices than other producers
They are exempt from price swings through government contracts
Profit is market price minus production cost, so the lowest-cost producers still earn a margin when prices fall
They hold more inventory than competitors
questions.prompt: Steel and mining prices are set by global markets, yet low-cost producers keep earning in downturns. Why?
